metadata.title: Finding Is Not Grading.
metadata.purpose: Show that retrieval and grading are different systems: the Variance Matrix (three axes, forced choice), the JSON verdict contract with n8n, and the directional case similarity search cannot catch.

beats.new_visual_element: Composer: the retrieval match, and what it does not prove
beats.narration_text: Namaste. This is Liam, narrating for Onkar Bhujbal, a software engineer. Week three of the Provenance Gatekeeper. Last week's retrieval works — it reaches into the vector database and comes back with the right row from the immutable ledger. But look hard at what that actually proves. It proves we found a document. It does not prove the model told the truth about it. A match is a search result. It is not a verdict. Finding is not grading. So this week we built the Evaluation Layer: it categorises the hallucination and hands a structured verdict back to n8n.

beats.narration_text: Here is the whole idea in one breath. Retrieval locates a claim; it never judges one. Something separate has to compare the claim against the ledger and name the error. That separate thing is the Evaluation Layer.

beats.new_visual_element: The variance taxonomy — three axes, each with a worked claim/truth pair
beats.narration_text: We grade every output against the Variance Matrix, and the logic must pick exactly one axis. Supported: the claim matches the ledger. Magnitude Error: the direction is right, but the number is hallucinated. Directional Error: the number is close, and the polarity is inverted — growth reported as loss. One claim, one axis, no hedging. That forced choice is the whole design.

shot.visual_intent: The three axes as stacked rows — the script's art direction — each carrying its rule and a worked claim-versus-truth pair, so the axis is defined by an example, not a label.

Row 03 DIRECTIONAL snaps in: down 12% against up 12%
Spark line lands: One claim. One axis.

beats.new_visual_element: The verify loop — n8n to FastAPI to ChromaDB to strict JSON verdict
beats.narration_text: Here is the contract. n8n posts the claim payload to a FastAPI webhook. The webhook pulls the matching ledger row out of ChromaDB, hands claim and truth to the grader, and the grader must return exactly one axis. It goes back as strict JSON — because the next node branches on a field, not on a sentence.

shot.visual_intent: The round trip performed: the claim payload enters at n8n, travels the stages, meets the ledger row, and leaves as a graded verdict. The model is nowhere in the loop — it is being graded.

beats.new_visual_element: The directional blindspot — one word apart, near-identical to a vector
beats.narration_text: So why a dedicated layer, instead of leaning on the similarity search? Because of the directional case. Minus twelve percent and plus twelve percent are almost the same string — vector math scores them as near-identical and passes the claim. The tokens match. The meaning is inverted. Similarity cannot see a sign flip, and a sign flip is the difference between growth and loss.

shot.visual_intent: The two sentences sit one above the other with only one word differing in colour, and the similarity bar fills almost full underneath — the eye sees why the search passes it.

beats.narration_text: Where week three landed. The grader takes three axes and must choose one. The transport is a FastAPI endpoint. The ground truth is a ledger row. The orchestrator branches on the axis field, not on a sentence. Retrieval finds, grading judges, and they are two different systems with two different failure modes.

beats.new_visual_element: Your turn — the cURL audit, typed and discussed
beats.narration_text: Your turn — audit the endpoint yourself. Post this to your local server: claim id test zero one, generated claim, Q3 revenue decreased fifteen percent. That claim is false; the ledger says revenue grew. Watch two things in the response. First, which axis it picks — it should be directional error, not magnitude. Second, the shape: every field the orchestrator needs, and nothing it has to dig out of a sentence. If the axis comes back wrong, your grader is wrong, and you found it in one request. And if it comes back as magnitude instead of directional, your grader is collapsing a sign flip into a size error — which is the exact bug this layer exists to catch.

shot.visual_intent: HANDOFF LAW: a prompt worth running, typed out, read aloud verbatim and then discussed — what to look for in the response — before the invitation to pause. The script's terminal command block lives here, in the brand's composer.
